text: A song of ascents. To you I lift up my eyes, to you whose throne is in the heavens.

versions.text: A song of ascents. To you I lift up my eyes, you who are enthroned in the heavens.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew participle הַיֹּשְׁבִי means literally "the one sitting/dwelling"; "enthroned" is a fair rendering but the current phrasing "you who are enthroned" is slightly heavy for oral reading. A smoother relative clause improves rhythm without losing the royal sense.

text: See how the eyes of servants look to the hand of their masters, how the eyes of a servant girl look to the hand of her mistress; so our eyes look to the LORD our God, until he shows us mercy.

versions.text: As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maid to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes look to the LORD our God, until he shows us mercy.
versions.explanation: The opening הִנֵּה ("behold/see") is untranslated, and אֲדוֹנֵיהֶם is plural ("their masters"). Adding the verb in the second clause also aids oral flow.

text: Have mercy on us, LORD, have mercy on us, for we have had our fill of contempt.
Our soul has had far more than its fill of the scorn of the complacent, of the contempt of the arrogant.

versions.text: Our soul has had more than enough of the mockery of the complacent, of the contempt of the proud.
versions.explanation: Repeating the imagery of "fill" (שָׂבְעָה, the same root as in v. 3) preserves the deliberate link between the two verses, and "arrogant" better matches גְּאֵיוֹנִים.
